Quite a while back, I started a topic on ficta in Lassus' Missa
Octavi Toni. My problem at the time was deciding whether a particular
bar contained a genuine cadence and hence would require or justify a
ficta alteration.
I'm currently looking at Tallis' "Oh Lord, in thee is all my trust".
The problem I encounter there is that there are quite a number of
spots that would qualify as a clausula (thirds and sixths leading to
fifths and octaves, if I recall correctly), but that it just seems
sooooo much, especially since the piece is actually composed of three
identical stanzas.

So here's the question to the collective wisdom: is it acceptable to
apply ficta to some clausulae rather than to others (e.g. at the end
of grammatical sentences, and not at subclauses), and if so, are there
any rules to govern that process? Or might I just as well flip a
coin?

I couldn't find an on-line edition or recording for common reference -
hope someone knows either the anthem in particular or the rule in
general.

Cordially

Martin Keller

>
> So here's the question to the collective wisdom: is it acceptable to
> apply ficta to some clausulae rather than to others (e.g. at the end

Hello, there, Martin.

Please let me emphasize that my generalized response to this question does
not take into account the specific time and place, as has been done in
another very helpful response, and should not be read to take priority
over those specific considerations.

Anyway, I would say that applying ficta (or also recta inflections such
as Bb) to some clausulae rather than others in the same piece is a
typical 16th-century technique documented by Robert Toft for certain
tablatures which show the precise semitone inflections intended. The
distinction between "grammatical sentences" and "subclauses" reminds me
of a suggestion by Gaffurius (1496) that one should apply inflections
at a cadence marking the conclusion either of the piece or of a section
of the text.

If you do choose to take this kind of approach, then your musical
intuition at the moment might be the best guide -- which some people
might regard as a "coin toss," but could also reflect a certain
intangible response to what sounds beautiful at the moment.

For a general discussion of these points:

<http://www.medieval.org/emfaq/harmony/hex.html>

By the way, Renaissance music often seems to follow the traditional
cadential formulae of the late medieval era, with minor thirds
often contracting to unisons, major thirds expanding to fifths,
and major sixths to octaves -- but with some modifications and
additions. For example, while the major third to fifth progression
often occurs in multi-voice music, it is less common as a definitive
cadence than the others. Also, a significant formulae in two-voice
as well multi-voice music (where it is often accompanied by other
two-voice formulae) is the suspension of a fourth or eleventh,
resolving to a major third or tenth, and from there to a unison
or octave with the upper voice rising a semitone and the lower
falling by a fifth or rising by a fourth.

Some writers of the middle to late 16th century such as Tomas de
Santa Maria, Zarlino, and Morley, seem to suggest that inflections
should be applied pretty much uniformly to all "closes" or similar
directed progressions, except if unacceptable complications (at least
for Zarlino) such as unwanted augmented or diminished intervals
should result. However, a lot of 16th-century practice is more
flexible.

Also, as for Tallis, I find quite credible the suggestion in another
reply that he may have wanted to specify accidentals fairly
comprehensively rather than leave them to performers. This is the
view of Pietro Aaron in 1529: that composers might well use
explicit accidentals as "signs of the road" so that performers
will not needlessly get lost.

Of course, creative variations in accidentals have their own
charm -- but it's interesting to ask what practice Tallis may
have followed or intended.

I believe that Martin is asking whether there is a hierarchy of
importance in analyzing 2-voice renaissance cadences, and I agree
with Laura that there very definitely is. Major cadences tend to
display only octaves, 4ths and 5ths, and almost certainly call for
ficta adjustments to give them added strength. Secondary cadences
would be those which mark the end of lines of text or points of
imitation, and would normally (in my experience) be similarly
inflected, but very often they are not full stops and are overlapped
by other voices creating other intervals, and therefore less strong.
The real question comes with apparent or potential passing cadences
in the middle of a line of text, and that is where modern
interpreters may well differ in their realization. I myself tend to
lean toward a more modal sound, and tend not to inflect passing
cadences. Other editors and other musicologists have taken a more
liberal approach that results in a great many inflections. The late,
great Karl Reinhardt tended to sprinkle Bbs throughout a manuscript if a
single Bb appeared anywhere in that piece! However, there is an
important caveat in basing one's analysis on text placement, and that
is the reliability or lack of reliability in the text underlay.
Someone claiming to be a student of Josquin said that the first thing
he did was to teach his choristers how to set he words to the music!

>If you do choose to take this kind of approach, then your musical
>intuition at the moment might be the best guide -- which some people
>might regard as a "coin toss," but could also reflect a certain
>intangible response to what sounds beautiful at the moment.

I believe--and the late Peter Langford flat-out stated--that we are
quite foolish to even imagine that there was ever a single, unvarying
way to perform ANY piece of renaissance music. Laura cites
instrumental tablatures, which are extremely valuable, but I don't
believe that various intabulations of the same piece necessarily all
agree with one another.

David Harper wrote:
>The Eton Choirbooks are fairly earnest in their notation.. the same
>way that Bach wrote out his ornamentations, knowing that some
>performers might be tempted to distort his intention.

In the case of Bach, one has to be careful about generalizations.
Yes, he wrote out the ornamentation in his keyboard works, which were
meant as teaching pieces and which are almost the only things
actually published in his lifetime. But my analysis of the St. John
Passion surprised me by showing that there were many more ornaments
written out for the soprano and alto arias, and many fewer for the
tenor and bass solos. One could argue that this proves he wanted
less ornamentation in those solos, but I see it as proof that he was
still teaching the younger singers proper style, which he expected
the older singers to understand.

>IMHO (and the real musicologists will correct me), Tallis set down
>quite accurately what he wanted to hear. This may not answer your
>question, but take a look at the source.

What source? You may be quite right that few ficta inflections are
needed or were expected in his music, but I would certainly not
accept that as an a priori axiom!! Unfortunately I have no Tallis
handy to analyze.

Laura:


>Some writers of the middle to late 16th century such as Tomas de
>Santa Maria, Zarlino, and Morley, seem to suggest that inflections
>should be applied pretty much uniformly to all "closes" or similar
>directed progressions, except if unacceptable complications (at least

>

>view of Pietro Aaron in 1529: that composers might well use
>explicit accidentals as "signs of the road" so that performers
>will not needlessly get lost.

Yes, which leaves the question where it must be left, and leaves
those of us who try to bring the pages to life making our own
decisions: "It depends!"

Michael

Michael, please let me agree with this comment most emphatically. One of
the things that Robert Toft shows is not only that different tablatures
can vary in their use of accidentals, but that within a single
intabulation of a given piece, the treatment of a passage might vary on
repetition. Thus not only is there no single authoritative interpretation
of a piece; there's not necessarily a single fixed interpretation for a
given performer.

Also, I recall in a modern edition of some of Verdelot's madrigals, the
editor gives both a vocal score and an indication of accidentals in a
version for lute -- noting that the latter has some progressions where
a major third expands to a fifth, or in traditional modern parlance,
"double leading-tone cadences" of a kind typical of the 14th and early
15th centuries. It's suggested that this effect might have been favored
more in a lute setting than an ensemble performance with voices, although
maybe "experiment and see what you like" might not be a bad conclusion.

Most appreciatively,

Laura Bennett

Hi, Philippe, and I also recall those passages in _The Notation of Polyphonic
Music 900-1600_ where Karl Reinhardt warns against indiscriminately adding inflections,
either in regard to _musica ficta_ or _musica recta_ (B-natural or Bb). He
urges that the logic and direction of the melodic line should be a vital
consideration, and suggests that the best alternative to his suggestions
might be an even more sparing approach to added accidentals.

Some of his views are rather confidential: for example, that late 15th-century
practice may have shied away from previously customary inflections, resulting
in a performance style of a kind we might now associate with the "German
custom" of the 16th century followed by some tablatures there which do often
leave important cadences uninflected. The Tallis Scholars did this kind of
thing quite pleasingly, at least to my taste, in one of their Josquin
performances, although critics might add that an early 16th-century ensemble
following this kind of practice would hopefully have been more accurate in
interpreting certain mensural signs (a favorite theme of certain reviews).

Anyway, an interesting example in HAM which I might consider more problematic
than is suggested by Karl Reinhardt (or Lowinsky) is Clemens non Papa's _Vox in Rama_.
There is a passage which _might_ have received a reading in the tenor of
Bb-A-G#-A, with the sharp suggested editorially and evidently taken as a
given in the editorial notes, which describe this as a "Neapolitan" cadence.
However, Bb-A-G-A is in my view also possible, and would result in a minor
third to octave progression between the two lower voices somewhat akin to
what Vicentino describes as the "gloomy" effect of a minor sixth expanding
to an octave -- quite fitting the text! True, following later 16th-century
theorists like Tomas de Santa Maria, the G# would presumably be preferable
to committing the "fault of rising by a tone" at a cadence with a suspended
eleventh or fourth. However, 16th-century practices vary, and what might
almost be termed the _understated_ rhetoric of that G-natural might have a
special appeal, at least as a variation to be used some of the time.

At least, the tablatures show that it's not unthinkable to leave certain
cadences uninflected -- so that what Karl Reinhardt says may sometimes suggest
credible alternatives to what he does in a given transcription, not so
surprising given the range of alternatives.

I'm interested in Tallis's motet "O nata lux de lumine". There's a
score here which I'll use for reference:

http://www.cpdl.org/wiki/images/2/2f/Tallis.pdf

I'm interested in some of the musica ficta practices that seem to have
become traditional in this piece. I'd really appreciate the advice of
anyone with expertise in this area.


The first place is on the Discantus (second line down), measure 1,
second note on the word "lux". Here is the text of the source:

G G G F E-flat* D
O na- ta lux

The E-flat is changed to an E-natural in every edition I know. The
change must be due to musica ficta. But what is the justification for
this change?

By comparison the Discantus has a similar note-pattern one bar later in
the second half of measure 2:

C B-flat* B-flat* A A G
Je- su re- demp- tor sae-

No one has suggested changing the B-flats to B-naturals here, yet the
pattern of intervals is identical to the one on "O na- ta lux"

The second place I'm interested in is in measure 4. The Discantus and
Tenor (4th down) parts goes as follows:


D E-natural F* G [DISCANTUS]

di- gna- re cle-

G G F* D [TENOR]


Why isn't there a ficta change on "re" from F-natural to F-sharp, at
least in the Discantus? I've never heard one performed, or seen one
in a printed edition, yet I would expect to see such a change based on
the note paterns. There is a similar false relation written into the
music in measure 11 on "pro per- di- tis".

Thanks for your help!

Andrew

The problem is that, whatever may have been done elsewhere, one cannot
demonstrate that any such rule applied to Tudor music. Stephen Clarke,
erstwhile Professor of Music at Exeter University, believes that
cadences in this repertoire were *not* sharpened, at least until we get
to the end of the century. Somewhere in the Proceedings of the Royal
Musical Association there is an interesting article by him arguing his
position and if you look through the volumes he has edited for the Early
English Church Music series you will see that he leaves them all
unsharpened. He has not has many followers, however.

He has a point insofar as sharpening the cadences in music of the Eton
Choirbook period often sounds inept, does a violence to the style and
sometimes cannot be achieved without introducing questionable
dissonances. At the same time I am sure there can be no doubt that
sharpened cadences were known: they are sometimes marked in the Eton
Choirbook, most commonly at the closing (harmonic) cadence of a piece or
section.

Where I think he may have been right is in denying that there was any
*rule* about such things. I suspect it is largely our modern musical
training that leads us to seek consistency everywhere - to pronounce
that *all* cadences must be sharp or all flat. I seriously doubt that
the Tudors thought like that until Byrd came along.

You only have to look at two main sources of Taverner's "Western Wind"
mass to appreciate the scribes' lack of consistency in sharpening the
leading notes of the main tune. If you don't know this piece, suffice it
to say that each movement is essentially a chain of variations on a tune
which is repeated several times. The tune is in "G minor" and has
several Fs. The two scribes are quite at variance about which of these
Fs they sharpen and which they leave alone (some have to be left alone
for harmonic reasons). The only way of making the tune sound consistent
throughout the mass is to leave all the accidentals out. It has been
suggested that this is how Taverner wrote it (because we like to think
that he must have been consistent), but in fact we cannot tell because
the two sources are both early Elizabethan and have updated the piece in
certain respects - exactly how far being a matter for debate. But at
least it is quite plain that neither of these two Elizabethan scribes
expected the tune to have consistent chromatic inflections throught.

The question comes up as to whether theorists such as Gaffurius were
influential in England, and if so to what extent. Gaffurius favors
the closest approach principle at significant cadences in the narrower
sense of final or sectional closes, as opposed to the earlier as well as
latter concept of any directed progression from an imperfect to a perfect
interval (for example in Prosdocimus, c. 1408 and 1413, as well as Zarlino,
1558).

Aaron in 1529 also considers closest approach the general rule, and discusses
the dilemmas of performers trying to apply unwritten alterations "on the fly,"
concluding that even the best singers, on first attempting a piece, can hardly
avoid "a little dissonance" in the process of trial and error. His conclusion
is that composers should smooth the "road" travelled by the singers by written
out their accidental signs explicitly.

That is always a possibility, of course, but I find it unlikely for
several reasons. First, there is the matter of the "composer's
intentions." Every single piece of early music was composed for
immediate use, in known surroundings, by singers and/or
instrumentalists well known to the composer. I freely grant that
said composer would have expected certain pronunciations, certain
application of the rules of ficta, and certain assumptions as to
tempo and proportions, because he knew how that particular group of
performers made those decisions. The point, however, is that music
was never composed solely for publication and dissemination, although
if the composer were well known and the music popular it might
eventually be published and disseminated, usually without payment to
the composer.

Second, once music came to be notated rather than passed on by ear,
it WAS possible to disseminate it, slowly at first when every copy
had to be individually hand written, later in quantity when Petrucci
and others proved a reasonably wide market for printed music. Which
makes it inevitable that the music (the notes on paper) would be
recreated by musicians and in places where a local dialect might
automatically guarantee pronunciation different from what the
composer might have expected, a local practice might result in rather
different choices in the application of musica ficta, and even tempos
might be taken differently because of local custom. It was Tom
Binkley's belief that because of exactly these factors, no piece of
music was likely to have been performed exactly the same way twice,
certainly when the composer was no longer present. (I do see
exceptions in the case of music performed often in a single time and
place under a single leader, like the Allegri Miserere that remained
secret until some precocious kid named Wolfgang heard it and wrote it
out!)

Third, the question arises as to whether the composer would have
cared in the slightest about different realizations of his music.
Don't forget that from the end of the 18th century to the end of the
20th we have seen a steady shift in responsibility for actual
performances from the performer to the composer. Concert artists are
no longer expected to--and indeed are no longer trained and capable
of--improvising their own cadenzas or adding their own ornamentation.
Too many conservatory students learn that they are expected to play
what's on the page, nothing less, and nothing more, when it is
obvious to many of us that even the most detailed notation cannot
encompass every last jot and tittle of what makes an exciting and
communicative performance. The early synthesizer programmers
discovered just how much is NOT spelled out in notation! Thus, we
know perfectly well that in the 18th century the realization of a
piece of music was the co-responsibility of composer and performer,
and it seems unlikely in the extreme that music in previous centuries
was treated any differently, with the individual performer probably
having even more responsibility and control the further back we go.

Musicologists are trained to seek out the "first" version, or the
"last" version, or the "definitive" version of a particular piece of
music, but in many cases those ideals simply don't exist. Not all
differences in manuscript copies can be blames on sloppy scribes.
The differences among intabulations of vocal pieces are very
instructive. And in the cases of Handel's operas and oratorios, EACH
version was the valid version for that time and place with those
particular singers.

But I've been wrong before!
